title: Chapter 102 — A Bower in the Arsacides
paragraphs: Up to now, in describing the Sperm Whale, I have mostly dwelt on the marvels of his outer appearance, or else, separately and in detail, on a few features of his inner structure. But for a large, thorough, sweeping understanding of him, I must now unbutton him still further: untie the laces of his hose, unbuckle his garters, unfasten the hooks and eyes of the joints of his innermost bones, and set him before you in his final state — that is to say, in his unconditional skeleton.

But what now, Ishmael? How is it that you, a mere oarsman in the fishery, claim to know anything about the underground parts of the whale? Did learned Stubb, mounted on your capstan, deliver lectures on the anatomy of the Cetacea, and with the help of the windlass hold up a specimen rib for exhibition? Explain yourself, Ishmael. Can you land a full-grown whale on your deck for examination, the way a cook dishes up a roast pig? Surely not. Up to now you have been a true witness, Ishmael; but be careful how you seize a privilege that belongs to Jonah alone — the privilege of discoursing on the joists and beams, the rafters, ridgepole, sleepers and underpinnings that make up the framework of leviathan, and, likely enough, on the tallow-vats, dairy-rooms, pantries and cheese-rooms in his bowels.

I confess that since Jonah, few whalemen have got very far beneath the skin of the adult whale. Nevertheless, I have been blessed with a chance to dissect him in miniature. On a ship I once belonged to, a small cub Sperm Whale was hoisted bodily onto the deck for his poke, or bag, to make sheaths for the barbs of the harpoons and for the heads of the lances. Do you think I let that chance go by without using my boat-hatchet and jackknife, breaking the seal and reading all the contents of that young cub?

As for my exact knowledge of the leviathan's bones at their gigantic, fully grown size, I owe that rare knowledge to my late royal friend Tranquo, king of Tranque, one of the Arsacides. Years ago, when I was serving on the trading ship Dey of Algiers and we called at Tranque, the lord of Tranque invited me to spend part of the Arsacidean holidays with him at his secluded palm villa at Pupella, a seaside glen not far from his capital, which our sailors called Bamboo-Town.

Among many other fine qualities, my royal friend Tranquo had a devout love for all matters of barbaric curios, and had gathered together in Pupella whatever rare things the more ingenious of his people could invent: chiefly carved woods of wonderful design, chiseled shells, inlaid spears, costly paddles, aromatic canoes — and all these set out among whatever natural wonders the wonder-laden, tribute-paying waves had cast up on his shores.

The most important of these was a great Sperm Whale that had been found dead and stranded after an unusually long, raging gale, with his head against a coconut tree whose drooping tufts of feathery leaves looked like his green spout. When the huge body had finally been stripped of its fathom-deep wrappings and the bones had dried to dust in the sun, the skeleton was carefully carried up the Pupella glen, where a grand temple of lordly palms now gave it shelter.

The ribs were hung with trophies; the vertebrae were carved with Arsacidean chronicles in strange hieroglyphics; in the skull, the priests kept an aromatic flame always burning, so that the mystic head again sent forth its vapory spout; while, hung from a bough, the terrible lower jaw swung over all the worshippers, like the sword hung by a hair that so terrified Damocles.

It was a wondrous sight. The wood was as green as the mosses of the Icy Glen; the trees stood high and haughty, feeling their living sap; the busy earth beneath was like a weaver's loom with a gorgeous carpet on it, the ground-vine tendrils forming its warp and woof and the living flowers its figures. All the trees with all their laden branches, all the shrubs and ferns and grasses, the message-carrying air — all these were unceasingly active. Through the lacework of the leaves, the great sun seemed a flying shuttle weaving the tireless greenery. Oh, busy weaver! Unseen weaver! Pause! One word! Where does the fabric flow? What palace will it adorn? Why all this ceaseless toil? Speak, weaver! Stop your hand! Just one single word with you! No — the shuttle flies; the figures float out of the loom; the carpet, rushing like a flood, slides away forever. The weaver-god weaves, and that weaving deafens him so that he hears no mortal voice; and that humming deafens us too, who look on at the loom; and only when we escape it shall we hear the thousand voices that speak through it. For it is just the same in all material factories. The spoken words that cannot be heard among the flying spindles are plainly heard outside the walls, bursting from the open windows. That is how villainies have been found out. Ah, mortal! Then be careful; for so, in all this din of the great world's loom, your most secret thoughts may be overheard far away.

There, in the green, restlessly living loom of that Arsacidean wood, the great, white, worshipped skeleton lay lounging — a gigantic idler! And yet, as the green warp and weft, forever being woven, mingled and hummed around him, the mighty idler seemed to be the cunning weaver himself, though he was all woven over with the vines, putting on greener and fresher growth every month, and was himself only a skeleton. Life wrapped Death; Death was a trellis for Life; the grim god married youthful Life and fathered curly-headed glories on her.

When I visited this wonderful whale with royal Tranquo and saw that its skull had been made an altar, with artificial smoke rising from the place where the real spout had come out, I was surprised that the king should treat a chapel as a collector's piece. He laughed. But I was more surprised that the priests swore that smoky spout of his was genuine. I paced back and forth in front of the skeleton, pushed the vines aside, broke in through the ribs, and, unwinding a ball of Arsacidean twine behind me, wandered and circled for a long time among its many winding, shady colonnades and arbors. But my line soon ran out, and following it back, I came out through the opening where I had gone in. I saw nothing living inside; there was nothing there but bones.

Cutting myself a green measuring-rod, I once more dove within the skeleton. From their arrow-slit in the skull, the priests saw me taking the height of the final rib. "What's this!" they shouted. "You dare to measure this god of ours! That's for us to do." "Aye, priests — well, how long do you make him, then?" But here a fierce argument broke out among them concerning feet and inches; they cracked each other's heads with their yardsticks — the great skull echoed — and seizing that lucky chance, I quickly completed my own measurements.

These measurements I now propose to set before you. But first let it be recorded that in this matter I am not free to state any imaginary measurement I please, because there are skeleton authorities you can consult to test my accuracy. There is a Leviathanic Museum, I am told, in Hull, England, one of that country's whaling ports, where they have some fine specimens of fin-backs and other whales. Likewise, I have heard that in the museum of Manchester, in New Hampshire, they have what the proprietors call "the only perfect specimen of a Greenland or River Whale in the United States." Moreover, at a place in Yorkshire, England, by the name of Burton Constable, a certain Sir Clifford Constable owns the skeleton of a Sperm Whale, but of moderate size, by no means of the full-grown magnitude of my friend King Tranquo's.

In both cases, the stranded whales to which these two skeletons belonged were originally claimed by their owners on similar grounds: King Tranquo seized his because he wanted it, and Sir Clifford because he was lord of the manors of those parts. Sir Clifford's whale has been articulated throughout, so that, like a great chest of drawers, you can open and shut him in all his bony cavities — spread out his ribs like a gigantic fan — and swing all day on his lower jaw. Locks are to be put on some of his trap-doors and shutters, and a footman will show future visitors around with a bunch of keys at his side. Sir Clifford is thinking of charging twopence for a peep at the whispering gallery in the spinal column, threepence to hear the echo in the hollow of his cerebellum, and sixpence for the unrivaled view from his forehead.

The measurements of the skeleton that I am about to record are copied word for word from my right arm, where I had them tattooed, since in my wild wanderings at the time there was no other safe way to keep such valuable figures. But I was short of space, and I wanted the rest of my body — or whatever parts of it were still untattooed — to stay a blank page for a poem I was writing then, so I did not bother with the odd inches. Nor, in fact, should inches come into any measurement of the whale that suits him.
